title: The Operating Feed
summary: The film stops being wallpaper and becomes the subject: the hero sits on the same flat graphite as every section below, and its one instrument is a framed, cinema-wide film of a working session in three takes, one per system Kelwin runs, with a measured chapter rail you can click.

reference.borrowed: Sunday: the film as a contained card on black with one quiet label, so it reads as R&D evidence, not mood. Atlas (refs/hero-r6-6.webp): framed footage with a strip of takes under it, so you know there is more than one shot. Lattice (refs/hero-r6-9.webp): one line of text inside the frame that gives the footage a voice.
reference.kelwin: The card becomes a hairline frame with four registration marks. The strip of takes becomes a calibrated ruler (one tick per second of the loop) with three clickable chapters named after the three capabilities, each marked with its nav glyph (CONTOUR, TRACE, ORBIT). The subtitle becomes one mono line: session, take, timecode.

video: What the mockup uses: there is no new footage, so the frame holds the same film plate as today's hero (img/film-room.webp) inside .km-film at the contract floor (blur 8px, light frost, the standard grain). It is graded darker and cooler than today's hero (deeper blacks, less sepia) so it reads as night-time cinema footage rather than a dim photo, and it is re-framed into three takes with hard cuts between them. Take 01 is close on the colleague leaning in at the wall. Take 02 is past a shoulder onto the seated figure, lit by the screen in front of him. Take 03 is wide from the other side: the man from behind, the room past him. Each take has one camera move (a push in, a sideways track, a pull back) and one footage cue: take 01 opens soft and pulls focus, the screen light on take 02 shifts as he works, and in take 03 someone walks past the glass. The plate is itself a mirror image, so every crop is kept to one side of the mirror line and no person ever appears twice in a frame. All of this is CSS keyed to the active take, with a small timer that makes the cuts and writes the timecode. There is no canvas and no per-frame script. How the real film would be made: a short commissioned shoot (4K, 24fps) of a real client working session, filmed through reeded or fluted glass, so the frosting happens in the lens. Gestures read but faces never do. That gives three 8-second takes: hands mapping a narrative on a wall (Narrative Systems), a screen of routing and sequence logic (GTM Infrastructure), and a weekly signal review around a table (GTM Intelligence). They are graded warm-graphite, framed for 2.39:1, and delivered as one 24-second muted loop (H.265 MP4 + VP9 WebM, about 4 MB, playsinline), with take 01 as the poster. Clicking a chapter just jumps the video to 0, 8 or 16 seconds.
motion: entrance (about 2s): the nav hairline draws and its two marks register. The label, the two statement lines and the red rule arrive with the kit's head choreography. The frame then plots in drafting order: dashed construction lines run along its top and left edges, the hairline outline closes, the four corner marks register, and the picture fades up on take 01. The lede, the audit note and the doors follow. The ruler then calibrates left to right (one tick per second), the chapters fade up, and chapter 01 latches with its CONTOUR glyph drawing itself.

orchestrated moment: a short establishing run through all three takes. At 3.6s a hard cut to take 02: the playhead jumps to the second major tick, chapter 02 latches and its TRACE glyph draws. At 6.4s it cuts to take 03 (ORBIT). Each take holds for about three seconds, long enough to read its chapter name, so the opening never flickers.

ambient (the only loop): after that the takes cut every 8 seconds on a 24-second loop. The playhead and the elapsed line travel linearly, the timecode counts, each take carries its own camera move and footage cue, and the film grain flickers. When the hero leaves the screen (or the tab is hidden), the film, the playhead and the clock stop where they are and resume on return.

interaction: clicking or tapping a chapter jumps the film to that take. Auto-cycling then stops for good (your 'let them skim' rule from the System section), and the chosen take keeps playing on its own loop. Hovering a chapter brightens it.
reduced motion: a still poster of take 01 with chapter 01 active. There are no cuts, no camera moves, no playhead travel and no timers. The chapters still work and switch between still frames.
addressed: The video is now the subject, not the background. It sits in its own cinema-wide frame with a timecode, three named takes and a chapter rail, the way a monitoring feed does in an operations room. That reads as proprietary and enterprise, not as an agency showreel behind a headline.
Each take shows one of the three systems Kelwin installs, so the film carries the offer: Narrative Systems, GTM Infrastructure, GTM Intelligence. Clicking a chapter jumps the film to that system.

The hero now speaks the same language as the sections you approved: flat graphite, a hairline frame with registration marks, a measured ruler and the nav's capability glyphs. It becomes the page's first instrument instead of its only photograph.

The statement and the lede sit on solid graphite, so they are fully legible whatever the film is showing. 'Request a System Audit' sits at 760–816px, well above the fold on a 1440×900 screen, and the whole hero, chapters included, fits that screen with air to spare.
There is no Pause film button, no caption strip and no figure numbering anywhere. The film stops on its own when the hero is off screen, and visitors who ask for reduced motion get a still frame.
notes: Stage 1440×960: nav 0–96 · label 148 · statement box 200–434 (116px, two lines) · rule 466 · feed 500–816 (cols 1–7, 755×316, the 2.39:1 cinema ratio) · ruler 828 · chapters 834–868 · about 90px of air below. Right bay (cols 8–12): the lede's cap line meets the frame's top edge, and the audit note sits directly on the doors. The doors' bottom lands on the frame's bottom edge at 816, so the bay and the picture share both edges. At 1440×900 the chapters end at 868, 32px above the fold. At 1280×800 (page zoom .889) the button sits at 676–726 and the chapters end at 772. Changes from the concept: (1) the lede leads the right bay beside the film it describes, and the audit note moves down onto the button it qualifies; (2) the doors align to the picture's bottom edge rather than the chapter row; (3) the frame is 2.39:1 rather than 2.2:1, which reads as cinema and gives the fold room; (4) take 03 is a wide shot from the other side of the room rather than the full plate, because the full plate shows its mirror line (two copies of the same person); (5) the opening run holds each take for about three seconds rather than 1.6s; (6) only the active chapter shows its glyph; (7) the mono line reads 'WORKING SESSION · TAKE 01/03 · 00:00:12' (39 characters). Flags: the chapter rail brings back a ruler and a timecode, which you removed from today's bottom band. They come back as the film's own controls inside the frame's column, with no caption text and nothing full-width, so this is not the old caption strip, but it is your call. The statement is anchored at the top rather than near the vertical centre, because the film takes the lower half. Marks: six in total (two on the nav hairline, four on the frame). Red: the two label squares, the rule and the primary button only. Gradients appear only inside .km-film (the slate scrim, the lens falloff and the screen light). The mono slate's worst-case contrast over the brightest frame is 7.1:1. Per your rule there is no Pause button, so for visitors who need the motion to stop, the reduced-motion still is the off switch; production should keep it. No new footage is claimed: the mockup reuses today's plate, and the meta says how the real film would be shot.
